Q: Forwarding a websocket call to my local machine A:

ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:3000 means smee reached your machine fine but nothing is listening on 3000. Check your container is actually publishing the port.

docker ps

Look for 0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp. If you only see 3000/tcp, you used EXPOSE without -p, so the port isn't published. Also confirm the app inside the container binds 0.0.0.0 rather than 127.0.0.1, since the latter is unreachable from outside the container.

If you need real websocket forwarding, use a tunnel that supports it, Cloudflare Tunnel and localtunnel both work too.

ngrok http 3000

Q: Why is my coroutine wrapper working when I use it as a decorator but not when I use it as a wrapper? A:

Your exception_handler takes a function and returns a function. As a decorator that's exactly right, since do_something is a function at class definition time.

But in _add_child_task, coro is already a coroutine object, not a function. Write a second version that takes a coroutine object.

async def with_handler(coro):
    try:
        await coro
    except CancelledError:
        logger.info("cancelled")
        raise
    except Exception as e:
        logger.exception(f"exception occurred - {e}")
    else:
        logger.info("completed successfully")

Then wrap the awaitable rather than the function.

def _add_child_task(self, coro: Coroutine, name: str = None) -> asyncio.Task:
    return self.create_task(with_handler(coro), name=name)

Q: Why do Binance/OKX offer historical trades but no historical order book (depth) replay, and what's the production way to get it? A:

Boss, Binance is handling millions of orders a second. If they stored every single micro-change (A -> B -> A) and let us download it, their AWS bill will go to the moon. They just drop the intermediate packets to keep their servers alive. So basically, exact historical replay doesn't even exist on their side to give us.

Since there's no history API, you have to build the book yourself in real-time.

  • First, you hit their REST API and download the full order book (the "snapshot"). It comes with an ID number called lastUpdateId.

  • But downloading takes like 1 second. In that 1 second, the market changed. So before downloading, you open a WebSocket (WS) live feed to catch the changes (diffs).

  • Binance sends these WS changes with a start ID (U) and end ID (u).

  • When your REST download finishes, you look at your WS buffer. You just ignore the old packets, and start applying the changes exactly where U <= snapshotID <= u. That's just their logic to stitch the live data onto the downloaded file without duplicating trades.

    BUUUUT , if If your internet drops even one single packet, your sequence breaks and since you missed an order, your local book is now corrupted, you literally have to clear your local and download a fresh REST snapshot to start again.

    So don't bother, just buy ready data from Tardis.dev, that's what industry does

Q: How is audio.duration calculated? A:

In JS, audio is powered by Web audio API.

The duration is calculated based on the audio context, sample rate, and the audio stored in the buffer.

"The duration property of the AudioBuffer interface returns a double representing the duration, in seconds, of the PCM data stored in the buffer." [mdm](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AudioBuffer/duration)

Q: How can I prevent duplicate JSON-LD schema output in WordPress? A:

The safest approach is to avoid generating a second LocalBusiness entity when Rank Math is already describing the same business.

Multiple JSON-LD blocks are not inherently a problem. The problem is having two separate entities that represent the same business but contain conflicting or redundant information.

With Rank Math, I would first inspect the final HTML source and determine what it is already generating. If it has a LocalBusiness/Organization entity, modify that schema through Rank Math's schema filters rather than outputting another <script> block from wp_head.

For example, Rank Math exposes filters that can be used to modify its schema graph:

add_filter( 'rank_math/json_ld', function( $data, $jsonld ) {

    // Modify the existing schema graph here.

    return $data;

}, 10, 2 );

The exact structure of $data depends on the schema Rank Math has generated, so I would inspect the array before modifying it rather than assuming a particular node/key exists.

If the information you need is not appropriate for Rank Math's existing entity, adding a separate JSON-LD block can be perfectly valid. In that case, give the entities stable @id values and reference the same business where appropriate instead of creating two unrelated descriptions.

For example:

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "LocalBusiness",
  "@id": "https://example.com/#business",
  "name": "Example Business",
  "url": "https://example.com/"
}

Then other schema nodes can reference that entity using:

{
  "@id": "https://example.com/#business"
}

So I would use this order of preference:

  1. Check the rendered HTML and identify every schema source.

  2. If Rank Math already creates the business entity, extend/modify that entity.

  3. If Rank Math cannot represent the required data, add a separate schema node and connect it with @id where appropriate.

  4. Remove redundant schema generated by another plugin/theme/custom code if it describes the same entity unnecessarily.

  5. Test the final rendered page, rather than only the PHP code, after clearing any page/cache/CDN layers.

Also, don't treat Google's Rich Results Test reporting multiple entities as proof that the JSON-LD is invalid. A page can legitimately contain multiple schema entities. What matters is whether those entities represent distinct things or whether several independent nodes are redundantly describing the same business.

In this case, I would not disable Rank Math's schema blindly. I'd inspect its generated graph first and modify or extend it where possible.
